vulnerabilities.Title: brace-expansion: brace-expansion: Denial of Service via stack exhaustion from crafted brace patterns
vulnerabilities.Description: The brace-expansion library generates arbitrary strings containing a common prefix and suffix. Prior to 1.1.19, 2.1.5, 3.0.7, and 5.0.10, crafted brace patterns can exhaust the native stack in parseCommaParts because parseCommaParts recursively processes the remainder once per brace group and uses push.apply to pass every element of a very large comma-part array as a function argument. Patterns containing many comma-separated brace groups trigger the recursive path, while the large array triggers the argument-array path without deep recursion. These paths cause recursive and argument-array native stack exhaustion before max or maxLength can limit output, potentially terminating the Node.js process in a process-terminating denial of service. This issue is fixed in versions 1.1.19, 2.1.5, 3.0.7, and 5.0.10.

vulnerabilities.Title: brace-expansion: brace-expansion: Denial of Service via uncontrolled recursion in nested brace patterns
vulnerabilities.Description: The brace-expansion library generates arbitrary strings containing a common prefix and suffix. Prior to 1.1.20, 2.1.6, 3.0.8, and 5.0.11, deeply nested brace groups cause expand_() to recurse once per nesting level at comma-member and single-set expansion sites, exhausting the native stack before output limits can apply and potentially terminating the Node.js process. expand_ performs uncontrolled recursion for nested brace alternatives and single-part sets. deeply nested brace groups supplied as an untrusted pattern. expand_ is affected. expand is affected. Comma members is affected. Single set is affected. native stack exhaustion during nested sub-expansion. process-terminating denial of service. This issue is fixed in versions 1.1.20, 2.1.6, 3.0.8, and 5.0.11.

vulnerabilities.Title: brace-expansion: Brace-expansion: Denial of Service due to exponential-time complexity
vulnerabilities.Description: brace-expansion through 5.0.6 is vulnerable to denial of service. The expand() function exhibits exponential-time complexity in the number of consecutive non-expanding '{}' brace groups. An attacker who passes a crafted string to expand(), directly or transitively, can cause significant CPU consumption and event-loop blocking. The max option does not mitigate this, as it bounds the output size rather than the recursion work.

vulnerabilities.Title: brace-expansion: Brace-expansion: Denial of Service via memory exhaustion in expand() function
vulnerabilities.Description: brace-expansion through 5.0.7 is vulnerable to denial of service via memory exhaustion. The expand() function limits the number of results with a max option (default 100,000) but does not bound the length of each result string. By chaining multiple brace groups, an attacker keeps the result count under the limit while making each result progressively longer, so total memory scales with both count and string length until the process hits a fatal, uncatchable out-of-memory error. About 7.5 KB of input ('{a,b}'.repeat(1500)) crashes a default Node.js process. Any application that passes attacker-influenced strings to brace-expansion.expand() - directly or transitively via minimatch / glob brace patterns - can be crashed by a small request. Fixed in 5.0.8 by adding a maxLength option (default 4,000,000) that bounds accumulated output and intermediate arrays.

vulnerabilities.Title: brace-expansion: DoS via unbounded intermediate arrays, bypassing the CVE-2026-14257 mitigation
vulnerabilities.Description: The brace-expansion library generates arbitrary strings containing a common prefix and suffix. Prior to 1.1.18, 2.1.4, 3.0.6, and 5.0.9, expand() does not apply maxLength while constructing comma-alternative intermediate arrays or padded sequences, allowing attacker-controlled input to exhaust memory or block the event loop. The fix for CVE-2026-14257 is bypassed by the vulnerability. This issue is fixed in versions 1.1.18, 2.1.4, 3.0.6, and 5.0.9.

vulnerabilities.Title: cross-spawn: regular expression denial of service
vulnerabilities.Description: Versions of the package cross-spawn before 6.0.6, from 7.0.0 and before 7.0.5 are vulnerable to Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) due to improper input sanitization. An attacker can increase the CPU usage and crash the program by crafting a very large and well crafted string.

vulnerabilities.Title: glob: glob: Command Injection Vulnerability via Malicious Filenames
vulnerabilities.Description: Glob matches files using patterns the shell uses. Starting in version 10.2.0 and prior to versions 10.5.0 and 11.1.0, the glob CLI contains a command injection vulnerability in its -c/--cmd option that allows arbitrary command execution when processing files with malicious names. When glob -c <command> <patterns> are used, matched filenames are passed to a shell with shell: true, enabling shell metacharacters in filenames to trigger command injection and achieve arbitrary code execution under the user or CI account privileges. This issue has been patched in versions 10.5.0 and 11.1.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: ip-address: ip-address: Inconsistent IP address parsing leads to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) and trust-boundary bypass
vulnerabilities.Description: ip-address is a library for parsing and manipulating IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in JavaScript. Prior to 10.3.1, Address4 accepts an octet written with a leading zero and decodes it as decimal, while the WHATWG URL host parser, inet_aton, and getaddrinfo all decode a leading zero as octal. The library and the network stack therefore disagree about which host a string names. new Address4('012.0.0.1') reports correctForm() of 12.0.0.1 and isPrivate() of false, but fetch('http://012.0.0.1/') connects to 10.0.0.1. An application that builds a network trust-boundary decision on these checks, for example a filter intended to block Server-Side Request Forgery, or SSRF, will classify an internal target as external and allow the request. The defect is in the parse gate rather than in any one classifier, so every consumer of Address4 inherits it: isPrivate(), isLoopback(), isLinkLocal(), isCGNAT(), isInSubnet(), isHostInSubnet(), and correctForm() are all computed from the mis-decoded octets. This issue is fixed in version 10.3.1.

vulnerabilities.Title: minimatch: minimatch: Denial of Service via specially crafted glob patterns
vulnerabilities.Description: minimatch is a minimal matching utility for converting glob expressions into JavaScript RegExp objects. Versions 10.2.0 and below are vulnerable to Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) when a glob pattern contains many consecutive * wildcards followed by a literal character that doesn't appear in the test string. Each * compiles to a separate [^/]*? regex group, and when the match fails, V8's regex engine backtracks exponentially across all possible splits. The time complexity is O(4^N) where N is the number of * characters. With N=15, a single minimatch() call takes ~2 seconds. With N=34, it hangs effectively forever. Any application that passes user-controlled strings to minimatch() as the pattern argument is vulnerable to DoS. This issue has been fixed in version 10.2.1.

vulnerabilities.Title: minimatch: minimatch: Denial of Service due to unbounded recursive backtracking via crafted glob patterns
vulnerabilities.Description: minimatch is a minimal matching utility for converting glob expressions into JavaScript RegExp objects. Prior to version 10.2.3, 9.0.7, 8.0.6, 7.4.8, 6.2.2, 5.1.8, 4.2.5, and 3.1.3, `matchOne()` performs unbounded recursive backtracking when a glob pattern contains multiple non-adjacent `**` (GLOBSTAR) segments and the input path does not match. The time complexity is O(C(n, k)) -- binomial -- where `n` is the number of path segments and `k` is the number of globstars. With k=11 and n=30, a call to the default `minimatch()` API stalls for roughly 5 seconds. With k=13, it exceeds 15 seconds. No memoization or call budget exists to bound this behavior. Any application where an attacker can influence the glob pattern passed to `minimatch()` is vulnerable. The realistic attack surface includes build tools and task runners that accept user-supplied glob arguments (ESLint, Webpack, Rollup config), multi-tenant systems where one tenant configures glob-based rules that run in a shared process, admin or developer interfaces that accept ignore-rule or filter configuration as globs, and CI/CD pipelines that evaluate user-submitted config files containing glob patterns. An attacker who can place a crafted pattern into any of these paths can stall the Node.js event loop for tens of seconds per invocation. The pattern is 56 bytes for a 5-second stall and does not require authentication in contexts where pattern input is part of the feature. Versions 10.2.3, 9.0.7, 8.0.6, 7.4.8, 6.2.2, 5.1.8, 4.2.5, and 3.1.3 fix the issue.

vulnerabilities.Title: minimatch: Minimatch: Denial of Service via catastrophic backtracking in glob expressions
vulnerabilities.Description: minimatch is a minimal matching utility for converting glob expressions into JavaScript RegExp objects. Prior to version 10.2.3, 9.0.7, 8.0.6, 7.4.8, 6.2.2, 5.1.8, 4.2.5, and 3.1.4, nested `*()` extglobs produce regexps with nested unbounded quantifiers (e.g. `(?:(?:a|b)*)*`), which exhibit catastrophic backtracking in V8. With a 12-byte pattern `*(*(*(a|b)))` and an 18-byte non-matching input, `minimatch()` stalls for over 7 seconds. Adding a single nesting level or a few input characters pushes this to minutes. This is the most severe finding: it is triggered by the default `minimatch()` API with no special options, and the minimum viable pattern is only 12 bytes. The same issue affects `+()` extglobs equally. Versions 10.2.3, 9.0.7, 8.0.6, 7.4.8, 6.2.2, 5.1.8, 4.2.5, and 3.1.4 fix the issue.

vulnerabilities.Title: pacote: Pacote: Denial of Service via crafted spec.rawSpec value in addGitSha function
vulnerabilities.Description: Versions of the package pacote from 11.2.7 and before 21.5.1 are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) via the addGitSha function. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by supplying a specially crafted spec.rawSpec value that triggers the function’s regex replacement and string-manipulation logic,  causing excessive CPU consumption and potentially stalling or crashing the process.

vulnerabilities.Title: sigstore: Sigstore: Unauthorized certificates accepted due to ignored `certificateOIDs` verification option
vulnerabilities.Description: sigstore-js provides JavaScript libraries for interacting with Sigstore services. Prior to 4.1.1, the documented certificateOIDs option in sigstore.verify() is accepted by the public API but discarded before verification, so required certificate extension OIDs are never checked and applications relying on certificateOIDs to restrict which certificates may sign artifacts can accept unauthorized certificates. This issue is fixed in version 4.1.1.

vulnerabilities.Title: tar: node-tar: Denial of Service via crafted gzip bomb
vulnerabilities.Description: node-tar is a tar archive manipulation library for Node.js. Prior to 7.5.19, node-tar does not enforce hard upper bounds on total decompressed data, entry counts, or decompression ratio in extraction and parsing paths such as src/extract.ts, allowing a small crafted gzip bomb to exhaust disk space and CPU. This issue is fixed in version 7.5.19.

vulnerabilities.Title: node-tar: tar: node-tar: Arbitrary file overwrite and symlink poisoning via unsanitized linkpaths in archives
vulnerabilities.Description: node-tar is a Tar for Node.js. The node-tar library (<= 7.5.2) fails to sanitize the linkpath of Link (hardlink) and SymbolicLink entries when preservePaths is false (the default secure behavior). This allows malicious archives to bypass the extraction root restriction, leading to Arbitrary File Overwrite via hardlinks and Symlink Poisoning via absolute symlink targets. This vulnerability is fixed in 7.5.3.

vulnerabilities.Title: node-tar: tar: node-tar: Arbitrary file overwrite via Unicode path collision race condition
vulnerabilities.Description: node-tar,a Tar for Node.js, has a race condition vulnerability in versions up to and including 7.5.3. This is due to an incomplete handling of Unicode path collisions in the `path-reservations` system. On case-insensitive or normalization-insensitive filesystems (such as macOS APFS, In which it has been tested), the library fails to lock colliding paths (e.g., `ß` and `ss`), allowing them to be processed in parallel. This bypasses the library's internal concurrency safeguards and permits Symlink Poisoning attacks via race conditions. The library uses a `PathReservations` system to ensure that metadata checks and file operations for the same path are serialized. This prevents race conditions where one entry might clobber another concurrently. This is a Race Condition which enables Arbitrary File Overwrite. This vulnerability affects users and systems using node-tar on macOS (APFS/HFS+). Because of using `NFD` Unicode normalization (in which `ß` and `ss` are different), conflicting paths do not have their order properly preserved under filesystems that ignore Unicode normalization (e.g., APFS (in which `ß` causes an inode collision with `ss`)). This enables an attacker to circumvent internal parallelization locks (`PathReservations`) using conflicting filenames within a malicious tar archive. The patch in version 7.5.4 updates `path-reservations.js` to use a normalization form that matches the target filesystem's behavior (e.g., `NFKD`), followed by first `toLocaleLowerCase('en')` and then `toLocaleUpperCase('en')`. As a workaround, users who cannot upgrade promptly, and who are programmatically using `node-tar` to extract arbitrary tarball data should filter out all `SymbolicLink` entries (as npm does) to defend against arbitrary file writes via this file system entry name collision issue.

vulnerabilities.Title: node-tar: tar: node-tar: Arbitrary file creation via path traversal bypass in hardlink security check
vulnerabilities.Description: node-tar,a Tar for Node.js, contains a vulnerability in versions prior to 7.5.7 where the security check for hardlink entries uses different path resolution semantics than the actual hardlink creation logic. This mismatch allows an attacker to craft a malicious TAR archive that bypasses path traversal protections and creates hardlinks to arbitrary files outside the extraction directory. Version 7.5.7 contains a fix for the issue.

vulnerabilities.Title: node-tar: node-tar: Arbitrary file read/write via malicious archive hardlink creation
vulnerabilities.Description: node-tar is a full-featured Tar for Node.js. When using default options in versions 7.5.7 and below, an attacker-controlled archive can create a hardlink inside the extraction directory that points to a file outside the extraction root, enabling arbitrary file read and write as the extracting user. Severity is high because the primitive bypasses path protections and turns archive extraction into a direct filesystem access primitive. This issue has been fixed in version 7.5.8.

vulnerabilities.Title: node-tar: hardlink path traversal via drive-relative linkpath
vulnerabilities.Description: node-tar is a full-featured Tar for Node.js. Prior to version 7.5.10, tar can be tricked into creating a hardlink that points outside the extraction directory by using a drive-relative link target such as C:../target.txt, which enables file overwrite outside cwd during normal tar.x() extraction. This issue has been patched in version 7.5.10.

vulnerabilities.Title: tar: tar: File overwrite via drive-relative symlink traversal
vulnerabilities.Description: node-tar is a full-featured Tar for Node.js. Prior to version 7.5.11, tar (npm) can be tricked into creating a symlink that points outside the extraction directory by using a drive-relative symlink target such as C:../../../target.txt, which enables file overwrite outside cwd during normal tar.x() extraction. This vulnerability is fixed in 7.5.11.

vulnerabilities.Title: tar: Node-tar: Denial of Service via malformed tar archive header
vulnerabilities.Description: node-tar is a tar archive manipulation library for Node.js. Prior to 7.5.18, tar.replace accepts a checksum-valid tar header with a negative base-256 encoded entry size, causing the archive scanner to make no progress while repeatedly parsing the same header. This issue is fixed in version 7.5.18.

vulnerabilities.Title: tar: node-tar: Denial of Service via crafted long-path tar archive
vulnerabilities.Description: node-tar is a tar archive manipulation library for Node.js. Prior to 7.5.21, node-tar's filesFilter in src/list.ts uses the recursive mapHas helper to walk an archive entry path upward with path.dirname() and no segment cap when tar.t(...) or tar.x(...) receives a non-empty member-selection list. A crafted GNU L or PAX x long-path header with thousands of slash-separated segments reaches this.filter(entry.path, entry) in Parser[CONSUMEHEADER] in src/parse.ts before Unpack[CHECKPATH] applies maxDepth, causing an uncatchable RangeError stack overflow that terminates asynchronous and streaming Node.js consumers. This issue is fixed in version 7.5.21.

vulnerabilities.Title: brotli: Out-of-Bounds Write in Google Brotli Decoder
vulnerabilities.Description:
A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.





Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.

vulnerabilities.Title: Scrapy: python-scrapy: brotli: Python brotli decompression bomb DoS
vulnerabilities.Description: Scrapy versions up to 2.13.2 are vulnerable to a denial of service (DoS) attack due to a flaw in its brotli decompression implementation. The protection mechanism against decompression bombs fails to mitigate the brotli variant, allowing remote servers to crash clients with less than 80GB of available memory. This occurs because brotli can achieve extremely high compression ratios for zero-filled data, leading to excessive memory consumption during decompression.

vulnerabilities.Title: anyio: AnyIO: TLS certificate spoofing via improper internationalized domain name encoding
vulnerabilities.Description: AnyIO is a high level asynchronous concurrency and networking framework that works on top of either Trio or asyncio. Prior to 4.14.2, connect_tcp() and TLSStream.wrap() can validate internationalized host names after the standard library converts them with IDNA 2003 instead of IDNA 2008. When a connection to a non-ASCII domain is hijacked or redirected, an attacker can obtain a legitimate certificate for the different ASCII hostname produced by IDNA 2003 and present it to the client, causing the malicious endpoint's certificate to validate. This issue is fixed in version 4.14.2.

vulnerabilities.Title: anyio: AnyIO: Privilege retention in child processes due to incorrect group handling
vulnerabilities.Description: AnyIO is a high level asynchronous concurrency and networking framework that works on top of either Trio or asyncio. In 4.14.0, AnyIO accepts the POSIX extra_groups argument in anyio.run_process() and anyio.open_process(), but open_process() forwards the group argument to the backend instead of extra_groups. A caller that supplies extra_groups=[] to clear inherited supplementary groups can therefore launch a child that retains the parent process groups, undermining a privilege-dropping boundary. If group is also supplied, the integer group value is passed where an iterable of supplementary groups is expected and the launch can fail with TypeError. This issue affects POSIX applications that rely on AnyIO subprocess helpers to launch less-privileged child processes. This issue is fixed in version 4.14.2.

vulnerabilities.Title: certifi bundles emSign root CAs with compromised intermediate CA keys
vulnerabilities.Description:
Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them. 

An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.

Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

vulnerabilities.Title: python-cryptography: python-cryptography: PKCS#7 EnvelopedData decryption exposes a Bleichenbacher oracle through distinguishable errors and timing
vulnerabilities.Description: cryptography is a package designed to expose cryptographic primitives and recipes to Python developers. From 44.0.0 until 50.0.0, pkcs7_decrypt_der, pkcs7_decrypt_pem, and pkcs7_decrypt_smime reported the outcome of decrypting a RecipientInfo's encryptedKey in several distinguishable ways, one of which disclosed the exact length recovered from the RSA operation. The same distinction was also observable by timing. An application that decrypts attacker-supplied EnvelopedData and reflects the outcome gives the attacker a Bleichenbacher oracle against the content-encryption key. Decryption ran as RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 decrypt of encryptedKey, build an AES cipher from the result, then AES-CBC decrypt and PKCS#7 unpad. Invalid RSA padding, a valid padding with a bad key length, a correct length with a wrong key, and the real key each failed or succeeded differently. Case 1 is reachable only where the linked library lacks implicit rejection: OpenSSL 3.0 and 3.1, LibreSSL, and BoringSSL. Exploitation requires a service that auto-decrypts untrusted EnvelopedData matching the victim certificate and answers adaptively at high volume, such as an S/MIME gateway or mail filter. This issue is fixed in 50.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: filelock: filelock: Arbitrary file overwrite via insecure database file reopening
vulnerabilities.Description: filelock is a platform-independent file lock for Python. From 3.20.4 until 4.2.1, ReadWriteLock let SQLite reopen the database and side files by name; on POSIX systems an attacker with rename access in a non-sticky parent can swap those names to cause overwrite or unlink operations, while a writable adjacent hot journal is additionally required for attacker-chosen content overwrites. This issue is fixed in version 4.2.1.

vulnerabilities.Title: httpx2: httpcore2: HTTPX2: WebSocket traffic sent in plaintext via SOCKS5 proxy due to TLS failure
vulnerabilities.Description: HTTPX2 is a next generation HTTP client for Python. Prior to 2.10.0, httpcore2 fails to start TLS in src/httpcore2/httpcore2/_sync/socks_proxy.py and src/httpcore2/httpcore2/_async/socks_proxy.py when the remote origin uses wss through a SOCKS5 proxy because the TLS upgrade condition only recognizes https. HTTPX2 exposes the flaw through Client.websocket() and AsyncClient.websocket() from 2.6.0 through 2.9.1, so the opening handshake, query parameters, Authorization headers, cookies, and subsequent frames can cross the proxy path in plaintext without certificate verification. An attacker controlling or observing that path can read or modify traffic and impersonate the WebSocket server. This issue is fixed in httpcore2 2.10.0 and HTTPX2 2.10.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: httpx2: HTTPX2: Denial of Service via streaming response decompression memory amplification
vulnerabilities.Description: HTTPX2 is a next generation HTTP client for Python. Prior to 2.12.0, the HTTPX2 content decoders in src/httpx2/httpx2/_decoders.py fully inflate each gzip, deflate, br, or zstd network chunk before iter_bytes() or aiter_bytes() yields bounded pieces to the application. A 64 KiB compressed chunk can expand to approximately 64 MiB in one intermediate allocation, so an attacker-controlled or compromised server can cause severe memory pressure or out-of-memory process termination even when the application streams the response. This issue is fixed in version 2.12.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: lxml: python: lxml: Information disclosure via untrusted XML input leading to local file read
vulnerabilities.Description: lxml is a library for processing XML and HTML in the Python language. Prior to 6.1.0, using either of the two parsers in the default configuration (with resolve_entities=True) allows untrusted XML input to read local files. Setting the resolve_entities option explicitly to resolve_entities='internal' or resolve_entities=False disables the local file access. This vulnerability is fixed in 6.1.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: MySQL Connector/Python connector takeover vulnerability
vulnerabilities.Description: Vulnerability in the MySQL Connectors product of Oracle MySQL (component: Connector/Python).  Supported versions that are affected are 9.0.0 and prior. Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows low privileged attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise MySQL Connectors.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of MySQL Connectors. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 7.5 (Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H).

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 2.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap buffer overflow and stale-heap disclosure in _tiffWriteProc when saving compressed TIFF data through libtiff to a target without a usable fileno(), such as BytesIO. The callback sizes its allocation from the prior buffer size instead of the current write position, allowing an attacker-controlled out-of-line TIFF tag or retained ICC profile to be copied beyond the allocation after libtiff seeks forward. This overflow can crash the process and may allow code execution. Independently, unwritten alignment gaps in compressed TIFF output larger than 64 KiB can disclose stale heap bytes without a crafted tag. File paths and targets with real file descriptors are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding leads to code execution
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's FlashPix JPEG-tile decoder can write decoded scanlines beyond the allocated tile buffer. FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding selects raw mode LA with two bytes per pixel, while an unrecognized JPEG mode can be decoded as JCS_UNKNOWN with four components, causing ImagingJpegDecode to write four-component scanlines into the two-byte tile buffer. An attacker can supply a crafted OLE2 FlashPix file to an application with the optional olefile dependency installed that opens or thumbnails untrusted input. This can corrupt heap memory and may allow arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in ImagingJpegDecode
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's JPEG decoder can write a full-width scanline into a buffer sized for a requested draft scale. ImagingJpegDecode does not verify libjpeg's actual output width and component count after scaling is requested, and an 8-bit lossless SOF3 JPEG decoded by a build linked to libjpeg-turbo 3.x can ignore the requested downscaling geometry. An attacker can supply such a JPEG to an application that uses draft() or thumbnail() to request downscaling. This can corrupt heap memory, crash the process, or potentially allow code execution. Older libjpeg-turbo 2.x and IJG builds reject the SOF3 input. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Argument Injection in Ghostscript call, potentially leading into RCE
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 2.6.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow is vulnerable to argument injection when invoking Ghostscript for EPS input. EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript passes a caller-controlled input filename after -f without converting it to a safe absolute path, so a name beginning with a hyphen can be interpreted as a Ghostscript option. An attacker who controls the filename can inject Ghostscript arguments. Arbitrary command execution specifically requires a leading @ argument-file filename and control of the referenced text file containing additional Ghostscript arguments; the reported chain reproduces with the default -dSAFER invocation. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, multi-fr ...
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, multi-frame loaders can retain an ImagingCore allocation created for a narrow frame mode while a later frame of the same dimensions changes the logical mode and decoder tiles to wider RGB or CMYK data. ImageFile.load_prepare() reuses the stale native storage because _im is non-null without verifying that its mode and size still match. Crafted PSD, MPO, DCX, or MIC frame transitions can then write wider pixels into the narrow allocation, causing native out-of-bounds writes and crashes. The MPO path can also cause a native over-read and, in demonstrated runtime-specific profiles, command execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via infinite loop during crafted MIC image parsing
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 7.2.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can enter an infinite loop while determining the frame count of a MIC image. MicImageFile inherits TIFF frame traversal, but MicImageFile.tell reports the OLE stream index and its seek() resets TIFF frame state, so an embedded TIFF with at least three IFDs never advances. When an application with olefile installed reads n_frames or saves all frames from a crafted MIC file, the non-advancing traversal can hold a worker at full CPU indefinitely. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via zero-size images in rank filters
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's rank-based filters can dereference invalid image storage for a zero-size image. ImagingExpand() allocates a non-empty output and then faults while replicating edges by reading the first pixel from empty input storage; ImagingRankFilter is never reached. An attacker can supply or cause creation of a zero-size image to an application that applies a rank, median, minimum, or maximum filter. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds memory access on zero-width images
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply() can access memory before a row buffer for a zero-width image. PPM and PGM input can create an image with width zero, and the native morphology routine indexes outrow[width - 1] without rejecting that geometry. An attacker can supply such an image to an application that applies a morphology operation. This can crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of service via crafted APNG image
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 8.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can allocate an APNG disposal background at the full canvas size before applying the decompression-bomb check. vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Memory disclosure and segfault in libtiff encoder via crafted TIFF tags
vulnerabilities.Description:
```
============================================================================
Memory disclosure and segfault in libtiff encoder via crafted TIFF tags
Location: src/encode.c:1014  in PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

A crafted TIFF file of a few hundred bytes makes Pillow copy an attacker-chosen amount of its own process memory into the TIFF it writes back out, or crash the process outright. The trigger is an ordinary `Image.open()` followed by a bare `im.save(fp, "TIFF")`. The only precondition is that the application re-saves images as TIFF. When the uploaded file is compressed, Pillow routes that save through libtiff automatically, with no options from the application. The attached reproducer does this with a 356-byte LZW TIFF: one crafted tag comes back holding 65536 bytes taken from `_imaging.so`'s read-only data, and a second crafted tag makes the worker die with SIGSEGV on every run.

The bug is in `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` (`src/encode.c`). It decides what arguments to pass to the variadic `TIFFSetField()` from the shape of the Python value (scalar, tuple or bytes). It assumes its `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo()` call defined how libtiff will read them. But `TIFFMergeFieldInfo()` never overrides libtiff's built-in field table, so libtiff reads the arguments according to its own definition of the tag:

- For a counted array tag such as DNGPrivateData (50740), a count-1 integer in the source file is taken as the byte count. The data pointer is then read from an argument slot Pillow never wrote, and that many bytes are copied into the output.
- For a fixed-size array tag such as ActiveArea (50829), the integer itself is used as the source address.

Where that unwritten slot points depends on the compiler. In the tested clang build it points into `_imaging.so`, and a larger count returned thousands of pointers into libpython, libc and libtiff, which defeats address-space randomisation for anyone chaining another bug. When the application preserves metadata with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2`, a 64-bit entry turns ActiveArea into a 16-byte read from an address the attacker chooses. All observed memory errors are reads; no out-of-bounds write was found.

Other branches of the same loop share the defect and are reachable from crafted TIFFs or from EXIF in JPEG/PNG/WebP re-saved as compressed TIFF. These are the `bytes`, RATIONAL-tuple and typed-tuple branches, and a BYTE-typed ColorMap. The file-reachable forwarding was introduced in `a3d45e9cefd0` ("Added custom int and float TIFF tags") and first released in 5.4.0.

## Details

`PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` (`src/encode.c:777-1060`) chooses the argument
list it hands to the variadic `TIFFSetField()` from the *Python* value of each
tag — scalar vs. tuple vs. `bytes`, and a type that is either autodetected or
copied from the source file's IFD — and assumes that its own
`ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo()` registration defines how libtiff will read the
`va_list`. It does not: libtiff keeps its built-in definition for every tag it
already knows, and core tags are never registered at all. libtiff therefore
consumes the varargs as `(count, pointer)`, `(pointer)` or three pointers
according to *its* field table, whatever Pillow actually pushed. The encoder
never consults that table (`TIFFFindField` / `TIFFFieldPassCount` /
`TIFFFieldWriteCount` / `TIFFFieldDataType`) before the call.

The most severe instance, and the one the attached reproducer exercises: when a
TIFF is re-saved through the libtiff writer, every tag of the source IFD that
Pillow does not recognise is forwarded to libtiff with `TIFFSetField()`. A
count-1 integer entry is passed as a single scalar vararg. If libtiff's own
field table defines that tag number as an *array* field, libtiff consumes the
varargs as `(count, pointer)` or `(pointer)` instead, so the attacker's integer
becomes either the number of bytes to copy from a never-written vararg slot, or
the source address itself. The same mismatch is reachable through the typed
tuple branches (tuple length consumed as a pointer for fixed-count built-in
tags such as `CFARepeatPatternDim`, even when the source file is well-formed),
the `bytes`, `TIFF_RATIONAL`-tuple and core-tag branches of the same loop;
those are listed
under *Other branches with the same defect* below and need to be covered by the
same fix.

A 181-byte TIFF (16×16 RGB, one LZW strip, plus one extra IFD entry
`50740 / LONG / count 1 / value 4096` — DNGPrivateData) opened with
`Image.open()` and saved with a bare `im.save(buf, "TIFF")` produces a 4296-byte
output whose tag 50740 holds 4096 bytes that occur nowhere in the input; scanning
`/proc/self/mem` finds them in the read-only data segment of `_imaging.so`.
Changing the extra entry to `50829 / LONG / 1 / 64` (ActiveArea) makes the same
two calls segfault in `memcpy(dst, src=0x40, n=16)` under
`ImagingLibTiffSetField` ← `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`. An ASan build of the
extensions reports `READ of size 4096` in `memcpy` called from
`src/encode.c:1014` for the first input.

### Code path

`_save` copies all tags of the opened image into the libtiff attribute list.
For a tag that is neither in `LIBTIFF_CORE` nor in `TiffTags.TAGS_V2`, no type
is recorded, so the value goes through untyped:

```python
# src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1782
supplied_tags = {**legacy_ifd, **getattr(im, "tag_v2", {})}
…
# :1959-1982
for tag, value in itertools.chain(ifd.items(), supplied_tags.items()):
    if tag not in TiffTags.LIBTIFF_CORE:
        …
        elif isinstance(value, (int, float, str, bytes)) or …:
            type = TiffTags.lookup(tag).type      # None for 50740, 50829, …
            if type:
                types[tag] = type
    if tag not in atts and tag not in blocklist:
        …
            atts[tag] = value                     # plain int 4096
```

`compression` defaults to the source image's `im.info["compression"]`
(`TiffImagePlugin.py:1731-1746`), so a compressed source selects the libtiff
writer without the application asking for it.

In the encoder the untyped `int` is autodetected as `TIFF_LONG`
(`src/encode.c:805-815`), the tag is "registered" as a scalar custom field, and
then set with one 32-bit vararg:

```c
// src/encode.c:844      (is_var_length = 0 → writecount 1, passcount 0)
if (ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo(&encoder->state, type, key_int, is_var_length)) {
    … continue;
}
…
// src/encode.c:1013-1016
} else if (type == TIFF_LONG || type == TIFF_IFD) {
    status = ImagingLibTiffSetField(
        &encoder->state, (ttag_t)key_int, (UINT32)PyLong_AsLong(value)
    );
```

The registration does not do what the caller assumes. `TIFFMergeFieldInfo()`
only adds definitions for tags libtiff does not already know and returns 0
(success) either way, so for tags in libtiff's built-in table the built-in
definition stays in force. Queried against the linked libtiff 4.5.0 after
exactly Pillow's merge call:

```
50740 DNGPrivateData      type=BYTE   passcount=1 writecount=-1   (unchanged)
50829 ActiveArea          type=LONG   passcount=0 writecount=4    (unchanged)
65000 CustomField         type=LONG   passcount=0 writecount=1    (Pillow's definition, tag was unknown)
```

libtiff's setter for `FIELD_CUSTOM` tags then interprets the `va_list`
according to *its* definition: for `passcount=1` it reads `va_arg(ap, int)` as
the element count — the attacker's 4096 — allocates `count * size` bytes and
`memcpy`s that many bytes from `va_arg(ap, void *)`, a slot
`PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` never wrote. On x86-64 that slot is register
`rcx`; in this build it holds a pointer into `_imaging.so`'s `.rodata`, so the
copy succeeds deterministically (a value of 2 000 000 also succeeds and yields a
2 000 200-byte output). `TIFFWriteDirectory` writes the copied bytes into the
output file as the tag's value. For fixed-count array fields (`passcount=0`,
`writecount=4` for ActiveArea) there is no count argument, so the attacker's
scalar is consumed as the `void *` source and 16 bytes are read from address
64 → SIGSEGV.

Tags in libtiff 4.5's built-in table that Pillow forwards untyped and that take
the `(count, pointer)` form include DNGPrivateData 50740, CFAPattern 33422,
CFAPlaneColor 50710, LinearizationTable 50712, BlackLevel 50714, WhiteLevel
50717, ColorMatrix1/2 50721/50722, AsShotNeutral 50728, OriginalRawFileName/Data
50827/50828, AsShotICCProfile 50831, CurrentICCProfile 50833. Fixed-count ones
(pointer only → crash) include ActiveArea 50829, DNGVersion/DNGBackwardVersion
50706/50707, DefaultScale/DefaultCropOrigin/DefaultCropSize 50718–50720,
AsShotWhiteXY 50729, CFARepeatPatternDim 33421, BlackLevelRepeatDim 50713,
ImageLayer 34732, RawDataUniqueID 50781.

When the application saves with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` (the documented way to
preserve metadata), the file-declared type is honoured, and a `LONG8` entry
reaches the `(uint64_t)PyLong_AsLongLong(value)` branch at
`src/encode.c:1049-1052`. For ActiveArea that is a 16-byte read from a full
64-bit attacker-chosen address into the output: a source entry
`50829 / LONG8 / 1 / <address of a Python bytes object>` produced an output
ActiveArea of `(b'SECR', b'ET-T', b'OKEN', b'-012')` in testing.

The comment above `blocklist +=` at `TiffImagePlugin.py:1938-1944` already notes
that array tags with the wrong length "will result in segfaults"; the blocklist
covers only a handful of tags Pillow itself knows, not the ones libtiff knows and
Pillow does not. Forwarding of these tags was introduced in `a3d45e9cefd0`
("Added custom int and float TIFF tags", 2018-10-25), first released in 5.4.0;
releases 2.0.0–3.0.0 forwarded them as scalars too, until `9fa6634f4`
("Partial fix for #1597") limited `_save` to `LIBTIFF_CORE`.

### Other branches with the same defect

The scalar-integer branch above is one of several places in the same loop
where the call shape is derived from the Python value rather than from
libtiff's definition. All of the following were confirmed on this commit (stock
build crashes and/or ASan reports, stack always `memcpy ← libtiff ←
ImagingLibTiffSetField src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:934 ←
PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`), and all are reachable from a sub-1 KB crafted
file followed by an ordinary `save()`:

* **Typed tuple → `(len, av)` for a fixed-count built-in field**
  (`src/encode.c:904-994`, the SHORT/LONG/SBYTE/SSHORT/SLONG/FLOAT/DOUBLE
  tuple branches all call `ImagingLibTiffSetField(..., len, av)`). For libtiff
  built-in fields with `passcount=0` and a fixed `writecount` —
  `CFARepeatPatternDim` 33421 (SHORT×2), `BlackLevelRepeatDim` 50713
  (SHORT×2), `ImageLayer` 34732 (LONG×2), `ActiveArea` 50829 (LONG×4),
  `MatrixWorldToScreen/Camera` 33305/33306 (FLOAT×16) — libtiff takes the
  *first* vararg as the source pointer, so the tuple length becomes the
  `memcpy` source address. A perfectly well-formed 206-byte 8×8 PackBits TIFF
  carrying `33421 / SHORT / 2 / (2, 2)` re-saved with a bare
  `im.save(out, "TIFF")` dies with SIGSEGV in `memcpy` (gdb: `rsi = 0x2`, the
  tuple length) on every run; so does
  `Image.new("L", (8, 8)).save(buf, "TIFF", compression="packbits",
  tiffinfo={33421: (2, 2)})`, and a JPEG whose EXIF carries the tag saved with
  `exif=im.getexif()` into a compressed TIFF. `bytes` values for built-in
  fixed-count BYTE tags (e.g. `DNGVersion` 50706, BYTE×4) crash the same way
  through the `(PyBytes_Size, PyBytes_AsString)` call at `src/encode.c:860-865`.
  The mirror image for `passcount=1` fields: `Photoshop` 34377 declared
  SHORT, count 1, value 60000 takes the scalar branch at `:1009-1012`, libtiff
  reads 60000 as the count and an unpassed vararg as the pointer, and the
  re-save *succeeds* with a 60162-byte output whose tag 34377 holds 60000 bytes
  of process memory (here C prototype strings from `_imaging.so`'s `.rodata`).
* **`bytes` value → single `char *`** (`src/encode.c:805-815` autodetects
  `bytes` as `TIFF_ASCII`; `:1033-1042` passes `PyBytes_AsString(value)` alone).
  `ImageFileDirectory_v2._setitem` stores a BYTE-typed entry as bare `bytes`
  and an ASCII-typed one as `str` (encoded to `bytes` by `_save`), so the
  file's declared type selects this branch.
  - `ColorMap` (320) declared BYTE with 4 bytes of data in a non-palette
    PackBits TIFF: 320 is in `core_tags[]`, no type is consulted, the value
    skips the 768-tuple `TIFFTAG_COLORMAP` branch (`:871-895`) and libtiff reads
    three `uint16_t *` and copies `1 << BitsPerSample` shorts from each — a
    512-byte over-read of the 5-byte Python bytes buffer, then dereference of
    two stale argument registers → SIGSEGV on every run of
    `Image.open(f); im.save(out, "TIFF")`. `COLORMAP` is not in `_save`'s
    `blocklist`.
  - `Photoshop` (34377) declared ASCII: `_save` copies value *and* type
    (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1802-1818`; only `IPTC_NAA_CHUNK` has a BYTE/UNDEFINED
    type guard there, from commit 2245df0a — `PHOTOSHOP_CHUNK` and `XMP` do
    not). libtiff's definition is BYTE, `passcount=1`, so the low 32 bits of
    the `char *` become the byte count for a `memcpy` from a stale register
    (ASan: `READ of size 3518384`; stock: SIGSEGV in about half of runs,
    otherwise `RuntimeError`). `ICCProfile` (34675) declared ASCII behaves the
    same way via `im.info["icc_profile"]` → `ifd[ICCPROFILE]`
    (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1822-1824`).
* **`TIFF_RATIONAL` tuple → array with no count** (`src/encode.c:995-1006`;
  compare the `TIFF_FLOAT` branch at `:969-981`, which passes `len, av`).
  - For a private tag (e.g. 50000) Pillow itself registers the field with
    `passcount=1` (`TiffDecode.c:904-908`), so libtiff takes the low 32 bits of
    `av` as the element count and the next stale vararg as the source:
    `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 119872 … right of 8-byte region` under
    ASan (`119872 == 4 * low32(av)`), SIGSEGV in ~4 of 5 stock runs. Reached by
    a JPEG whose EXIF carries one private RATIONAL×2 tag saved with
    `im.save(out, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", exif=im.info["exif"])`, or a
    TIFF re-saved with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` (`_setitem` auto-types a tuple of
    `IFDRational` as RATIONAL, `TiffImagePlugin.py:689-701`; `types[tag] =
    ifd.tagtype[tag]` at `:1968`).
  - For libtiff's built-in fixed-count float tags `WhitePoint` (318, 2),
    `PrimaryChromaticities` (319, 6) and `YCbCrCoefficients` (529, 3), which
    `_save` forwards from any source TIFF and types RATIONAL via
    `TiffTags.lookup`, the pointer-only convention happens to match, but
    libtiff copies its *fixed* count from an array that is only as long as the
    file declared: a PackBits TIFF with `PrimaryChromaticities` count 1 and a
    bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` gives `READ of size 24 … right of 4-byte
    region`, and the over-read floats are written to tag 319 of the output.
    `REFERENCEBLACKWHITE`/`TRANSFERFUNCTION` are blocklisted at
    `TiffImagePlugin.py:1941-1952` for exactly this reason; 318/319/529 are not.
* **Core tag reached as a scalar via a stale file-supplied type.** With the
  re-save idiom `im.save(out, "TIFF", tiffinfo=im.tag_v2)`, `_save` copies
  `ifd.tagtype[key] = info.tagtype[key]` for every key
  (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1768-1776`) and later assigns its own values to some of
  the same tags without resetting the type (`ifd[COLORMAP] = colormap` at
  `:1870-1877`; likewise BitsPerSample, SamplesPerPixel, ExtraSamples,
  ICCProfile, …). For a 418-byte PackBits *palette* TIFF whose ColorMap entry
  is declared BYTE, `_setitem` (`:751-770`) truncates `_save`'s 768-entry
  palette to a single `int` (with only a "too many entries" warning), the
  encoder receives `(320, 0)`, autodetects `TIFF_LONG`, and
  `src/encode.c:1013-1016` calls `TIFFSetField(TIFFTAG_COLORMAP, (UINT32)0)` —
  libtiff reads three `uint16_t *` and faults at an address ≤ 65280 on every
  run. The stale-tagtype copy is a Python-side hygiene bug in its own right,
  but its memory-safety consequence exists only because the encoder lets a
  non-tuple value reach `TIFFSetField(COLORMAP)`.

## Impact

Any service that accepts a TIFF and writes it back out as TIFF through libtiff —
which happens with a plain `im.save(fp, "TIFF")` whenever the uploaded file is
compressed, or whenever a `compression=` other than raw is requested — returns
to the uploader, inside one metadata tag of the produced file, an
attacker-chosen number of bytes read from a stale pointer in the worker process,
deterministically and without retries. Which memory that is depends on the
compiler's register allocation for `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`: in this clang
build the pointer is `_imaging.so + 0x1588`, so a request for 262 144 bytes
(which succeeded every time in testing, as did 2 000 000) covers the
extension's `.rodata`, `.data.rel.ro`/GOT and `.data` and returned 2 800+
resolved pointers into libpython, libc, libtiff, libjpeg and others — a complete
ASLR bypass for chaining with any other memory bug; a gcc build of the same
source left a different, unrelated address in that slot. The fixed-count
variant kills the worker process with SIGSEGV from a 181-byte upload on every
request. With `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` the source
address is fully attacker-chosen (16-byte arbitrary read into the output for
ActiveArea, or a crash). No non-default Pillow setting is involved; the only
precondition is TIFF-to-TIFF re-encoding.

The other branches add further deterministic process-kill inputs (BYTE-typed
ColorMap in any RGB or palette TIFF; `thumbnail()` keeps `tag_v2`, so
open→thumbnail→save-as-TIFF is affected too) and extend the reach to
JPEG/PNG/WebP uploads whose EXIF is preserved with `exif=` when converting to
libtiff-compressed TIFF. All the memory errors are reads; libtiff sizes its
destination buffers with the same count it copies, so no out-of-bounds write
was found.

## Reproducing

`repro` is one Python script, run against the stock build with the installed `PIL`. It needs no compiler and no extra files.

`upload(tag, value)` has Pillow write a 16×16 red RGB image as an LZW-compressed TIFF, then appends a new IFD holding the same entries plus one extra `<tag> / LONG / count 1 / value` (kept in tag order) and points the header at it — a 356-byte input on this tree. The source is LZW-compressed on purpose. A bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` keeps the source's compression, so the save goes through the libtiff writer even though the application passes no arguments. `resave()` is the whole "application": `Image.open(BytesIO(src)); im.save(out, "TIFF")`.

The script runs three cases:

1. **Control, tag 65000 = 4096.** libtiff does not know this tag, so the file is re-saved correctly and the output tag reads back as the integer `4096`. This is what should happen to every tag.
2. **Leak, DNGPrivateData 50740 = 65536.** libtiff's built-in definition of this tag is a counted BYTE array. It reads Pillow's single scalar as the *count* and takes the data pointer from a vararg slot Pillow never wrote. The output tag comes back as `bytes` of length 65536 that do not occur in the input. The script prints the first 32 of them and the file offset at which they occur in `_imaging.so` on disk. On this build they always do (offset `0x57588`): the stale pointer aims into the extension's read-only data.

## Suggested fix

The encoder must not guess the calling convention; it has to ask libtiff what
the tag's effective definition is *after* `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo` and
marshal accordingly, or refuse. The attached patch does this for non-core tags:

* a new `ImagingLibTiffFindField()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` (declared
  in `TiffDecode.h`, next to the other libtiff wrappers) returns libtiff's
  `TIFFFindField` type, `passcount` and `writecount` for a tag;
* in `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` (`src/encode.c`), for a non-core tag that
  libtiff already knows, Pillow adopts libtiff's type when it has none of its
  own, and after `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo` a new `tiff_field_matches()`
  checks the value against libtiff's definition: a scalar only for a
  single-value field whose C argument type (int / `uint64_t` / double /
  `char *`) matches, an array only with libtiff's element size and, for
  fixed-count fields, exactly `writecount` elements. Anything else raises
  `ValueError("Tag value does not match libtiff field definition")` instead of
  reaching `TIFFSetField` — this covers the reproducer's DNGPrivateData and
  ActiveArea inputs, ASCII-typed Photoshop, short PrimaryChromaticities and the
  `LONG8` `tiffinfo=` variant;
* every tuple/`bytes` branch now goes through `set_tiff_array_field()`, which
  passes `len` only when the field has `passcount` set; this also fixes the
  `TIFF_RATIONAL` branch, which never passed a count (and extends it to
  `TIFF_SRATIONAL`);
* `TIFF_UNDEFINED` fields are registered as variable-length, matching how their
  `bytes` values are passed;
* `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` gains a regression test (scalar DNGPrivateData,
  scalar and 2-tuple ActiveArea rejected; well-formed values round-trip).

Core tags and tags libtiff does not know keep their current behaviour. With the
patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the reproducer no longer
triggers and the test suite passes. It is not a complete fix, however: the
whole check sits inside `if (!is_core_tag)`, so the BYTE-typed ColorMap variant
stays open. The PackBits RGB TIFF carrying `320 / BYTE / 4`, re-saved with a
bare `save()`, no longer segfaults at this point but writes 1536 bytes —
over-read from the 5-byte `bytes` object and two stale varargs, including 22
live heap pointers — into the output ColorMap, which is still a disclosure.
Before merging, it needs a guard that accepts `TIFFTAG_COLORMAP` only through
the existing 768-tuple branch, never through the scalar or `bytes` branches,
and ideally the same shape check for the other core tags libtiff special-cases
in `_TIFFVSetField` (YCbCrSubsampling 530, TransferFunction 301,
ReferenceBlackWhite 532).

Narrower Python-side mitigations in `_save` close individual entry points but
not the class, and are worth adding alongside the C-side check: drop tags
with `TiffTags.lookup(tag).type is None` from `supplied_tags` (closes the `Image.open()→save()` path shown here but not
`tiffinfo=` callers); remove `COLORMAP` from `supplied_tags` next to
`EXIFIFD`/`SAMPLEFORMAT` and extend the `IPTC_NAA_CHUNK` BYTE/UNDEFINED type
guard to `PHOTOSHOP_CHUNK` and `XMP`; add 318/319/529 to the blocklist next to
`REFERENCEBLACKWHITE`; and have `_save` `ifd.tagtype.pop(tag, None)` before
assigning its own ColorMap/BitsPerSample/ICCProfile/… values so a
`tiffinfo=`-imported type cannot reshape them. The C-side check is the fix to
rely on.
